introduction-the-on-demand-trap.core: On-demand is the most flexible and most expensive price. Steady workloads left on on-demand overpay 30–70%. Commit for baseline usage, and use spot for interruptible work.

first_principles.problem: A company runs its always-on production fleet at on-demand rates for years.

analogy.title: Hotel rack rates
analogy.story: Paying the walk-in rate every night for a year-long stay instead of negotiating a long-term lease.
analogy.breaks: Over-committing wastes money if usage drops.

example.title: A layered compute purchase
example.outcome: each workload is paid for at the right price.

check.q: What workloads belong on on-demand pricing?
check.a: Variable or unpredictable usage that doesn't justify a commitment and can't tolerate interruption.

reserved-instances-ris-the-old-school-co.core: A Reserved Instance is a billing discount coupon (not a server) that automatically applies to matching usage (instance family, region, OS) for 1 or 3 years. Standard RIs give the deepest discounts but are rigid.

first_principles.problem: Teams buy RIs for the wrong instance types, then migrate and are left paying for unused reservations.
truths: The discount applies only to matching usage.
Longer terms and upfront payment give bigger discounts.
derivation: **Term** 1 or 3 years; **payment**: all, partial or no upfront.

analogy.title: A gym membership for a specific branch
analogy.story: It's cheaper than drop-ins, but useless if you move across town.
analogy.breaks: RIs still matter for RDS, ElastiCache and others, where Savings Plans don't apply.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Stable databases are discounted without architecture changes.

check.q: Is a Reserved Instance a physical server?
check.a: No. It's a billing discount that applies to matching usage.

savings-plans-the-modern-commitment.core: A Savings Plan commits to a dollar amount of compute per hour (for example $50/hr for 1 or 3 years) and discounts any eligible usage up to that amount. Compute Savings Plans apply across families, regions, Fargate and Lambda.

first_principles.problem: RIs break whenever you change instance type, region or move to containers.
truths: Spend commitments are more flexible than instance commitments.
derivation: **Compute SP**: any family, region, Fargate, Lambda.
**EC2 Instance SP**: one family per region, deeper discount.
Commit to the **stable floor** of spend.

analogy.title: A prepaid mobile data bundle
analogy.story: You commit to spending £30 a month and use it on any app, rather than reserving a specific app.
analogy.breaks: Commitments are hourly. An idle hour's commitment is lost, not rolled over.

example.title: Sizing a commitment
example.outcome: flexible discounts that survive architectural change.

check.q: Why commit to the minimum rather than the average hourly spend?
check.a: Commitment is billed every hour, so anything above actual usage is wasted.

the-spot-market-using-the-clearance-aisl.core: Spot sells unused capacity at up to 90% off, but the provider can reclaim it with a 2-minute warning. It's ideal for stateless, fault-tolerant, flexible workloads, diversified across many instance types and AZs.

first_principles.problem: Batch and CI fleets run at on-demand prices even though they could tolerate interruptions.
truths: Clouds keep excess capacity for peaks.
derivation: Use spot for **stateless, retryable** work (CI, batch, stateless web behind an LB).

analogy.title: A supermarket clearance aisle
analogy.story: Great prices, but the stock might be gone tomorrow, so don't rely on it for essentials.
analogy.breaks: Stateful singletons (primary databases) are a bad fit.

example.title: A CI runner fleet on spot
example.outcome: flexible workloads run for a fraction of the cost.

check.q: Why diversify spot instance types and AZs?
check.a: To reduce the chance that all capacity is reclaimed at once and to widen the pool you can draw from.

enterprise-agreements-and-the-marketplac.core: Large spenders negotiate private pricing (AWS EDP, Azure MACC, GCP commits): an overall spend commitment for an extra discount. Marketplace purchases can count toward those commitments.

first_principles.problem: A company spending $20M a year pays public prices and buys SaaS outside the cloud marketplace, missing commitment burn-down.
truths: Commitments reduce provider risk, which they reward.
Marketplace spend can draw down commitments.
derivation: Negotiate an **EDP/MACC** for a multi-year spend commitment.
**Route SaaS purchases** through the marketplace to burn down the commitment.

analogy.title: A corporate travel agreement
analogy.story: Commit to $5M a year with an airline and get 15% off every flight; bookings through partner hotels also count.
analogy.breaks: Over-committing creates shortfall payments, and lock-in reduces leverage later.

check.q: Why route SaaS purchases through the cloud marketplace?
check.a: They often count toward the committed spend in the enterprise agreement.
